prompt: What does `go mod init example.com/accents` ask of the network?
hint: Section 02 says what the path is checked for.

choices.text: It asks `example.com` whether the name is free
choices.why: Nothing visits the path; `example.com` is reserved for examples and answers nobody's go command.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. The path is a name, checked for its shape; it becomes an address only when somebody downloads the module.

choices.text: It reserves the path on the module proxy
choices.why: The proxy serves published modules; nothing is registered there by `init`.

choices.text: It records the new module in the checksum database
choices.why: The database holds hashes of versions somebody downloaded; a module nobody has fetched is not in it.

prompt: A colleague names a module `tools`, and another module imports its package `tools/lint`. What does `go build` in the second module do?
hint: Where did the go command look for `hello/greet`?

choices.text: Downloads `tools` from the module proxy and builds
choices.why: A first element with no dot is never sent to the proxy at all.

choices.text: Fails: `tools/lint` is not in the standard library
choices.why: Right. A path whose first element has no dot is looked up in `/usr/local/go/src`, as `hello/greet` was.

choices.text: Builds, because any module path of the right shape can be imported
choices.why: The right shape is enough for `init`, not for an import from another module.

choices.text: Asks for `go mod tidy`, which then adds a `require` line
choices.why: There is no module to require: the go command treats the path as part of the standard library.

prompt: Docker's latest version printed as `v28.5.2+___`, because its repository is past v1 and has no `go.mod`.
hint: A word that says the version carries none of a module's promises.

prompt: You will publish a library at `github.com/ana/textkit` next month, and the repository does not exist yet. What should `go mod init` get today?
hint: What does renaming a module cost later?

choices.text: An `example.com` path, renamed on publishing day
choices.why: Renaming means editing every import of the module's packages; choosing the real path now costs nothing.

choices.text: A short word with no dot, quicker to type
choices.why: A first element with no dot is read as the standard library, so nobody else could import it.

choices.text: The address it will be published at
choices.why: Right. `init` checks only the shape, and the path is where the go command will look once it is published.

choices.text: The full URL, with `https://` in front
choices.why: A module path has no scheme; `init` refuses characters a path may not contain, as it refused the space.

prompt: Lesson 1 printed `github.com/prometheus/prometheus v0.315.0`. Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the version as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.

choices.text: Its major version is 0
choices.why: Yes: `v0.315.0` is major 0, minor 315, patch 0.

choices.text: It promises no compatibility from one release to the next
choices.why: Yes. Major 0 makes no compatibility promise at all.

choices.text: Its path should end in `/v0`
choices.why: The suffix starts at major 2; v0 and v1 paths carry none.

choices.text: It is marked `+incompatible`
choices.why: That mark is for repositories tagged v2 or above with no `go.mod`; this version is major 0.

prompt: Where does a Go module first say that it depends on `golang.org/x/text`?
hint: What did `go mod tidy` read before it wrote anything?

choices.text: In `go.sum`, which lists every dependency's hash
choices.why: `go.sum` is written after the dependency is found; it records bytes, not intentions.

choices.text: In an `import` line of a `.go` file
choices.why: Right. The import is the declaration, and `tidy` writes `go.mod` to match it.

choices.text: In a manifest you edit before writing the import
choices.why: That is the habit of other package managers; `go.mod` was written by `tidy` from the import.

choices.text: In `go.work`, beside the module
choices.why: A workspace says how local modules are arranged on disk; it requires nothing from the network.

prompt: `go.sum` has two lines for `golang.org/x/text v0.42.0`. What does the one written `v0.42.0/go.mod h1:...` hash?
hint: The other line covers the module's files.

choices.text: Your own module's `go.mod`
choices.why: Your `go.mod` is not downloaded, so there is nothing to compare it with.

choices.text: The same zip again, with a stronger method
choices.why: Both lines say `h1:`, the same method; they cover different files.

choices.text: The `go.mod` file of `golang.org/x/text` alone
choices.why: Right. The first line hashes the module's files, the second only its `go.mod`.

choices.text: The list of versions the proxy offered for the module
choices.why: A list changes every release; `go.sum` holds hashes that never change for a version.

prompt: When does the go command ask `sum.golang.org` about a module version?
hint: `modfetch/fetch.go` decides it.

choices.text: On every build, before compiling any dependency
choices.why: After the first time, builds compare the cache with `go.sum` and ask no one.

choices.text: When it meets a hash that `go.sum` does not have yet
choices.why: Right. Once the hash is in `go.sum`, `go.sum` is the reference.

choices.text: Only when you run `go mod verify`
choices.why: `verify` checks the cache against what was downloaded; the database is consulted while downloading.

choices.text: Never: it exists for people to query with `curl`
choices.why: `go env GOSUMDB` named it because the go command uses it; `curl` only showed what it answers.

prompt: A teammate deletes `go.sum` from the repository to reduce noise. What happens when the next person clones it and runs `go build`?
hint: The build needs a hash for every module it compiles.

choices.text: It builds as before, since `go.mod` still names the versions
choices.why: A version names which release, not which bytes; the build refuses a module with no hash.

choices.text: It stops at `missing go.sum entry` until somebody runs `go mod tidy`
choices.why: Right, and that `tidy` takes the hashes afresh from whatever is downloaded that day, checked only by the database.

choices.text: It prints `SECURITY ERROR`, as when a hash was changed
choices.why: `SECURITY ERROR` needs two hashes that disagree; with no `go.sum` there is only one.

choices.text: It downloads the newest versions, since nothing pins them
choices.why: `go.mod` pins the versions; `go.sum` only pins their bytes.

prompt: Your module requires `example.com/a v1.2.0`. Another module you require needs `example.com/a v1.4.0`, and the latest release of `a` is v1.6.0. Which version does the build use?
hint: The highest of the stated minimums.

choices.text: v1.6.0, the latest
choices.why: Minimal version selection never picks a version nobody asked for; `x/tools` stayed at v0.49.0 with v0.51.0 out.

choices.text: v1.2.0, because your own `go.mod` wins
choices.why: The other module does not work below v1.4.0, and the rule takes every module's minimum into account.
Right. Each module states the lowest version it works with, and the go command takes the highest of those.

choices.text: None: the build stops and asks you to choose one of the two
choices.why: Two minimums are not a conflict; the higher one satisfies both modules.

prompt: Put in order what the first `go mod tidy` did for `golang.org/x/text`.
hint: The figure in section 03 draws it.
items: Read `main.go` and found an import no module provides
Asked the proxy which module provides the package, and its latest version
Checked the hash against the checksum database

prompt: `go mod tidy -___` prints the changes `tidy` would make, changes nothing, and exits 1 if there are any.
hint: The flag's name is the name of the format it prints.

prompt: What did `go mod vendor` copy into `vendor/`?
hint: Count the files `find` listed.

choices.text: The whole of `golang.org/x/text`, every package in it
choices.why: The module has 487 files; `vendor` got 14.

choices.text: The packages the build needs, with the licence files
choices.why: Right: `norm`, the `transform` it imports, `LICENSE` and `PATENTS`, and an index, `modules.txt`.

choices.text: A link to the module cache
choices.why: The point of `vendor` is to build with no cache at all; it holds real files.

choices.text: The hashes from `go.sum`, to check the cache against
choices.why: The hashes stay in `go.sum`; `vendor` holds source code.

prompt: `go mod vendor` copied 14 files of a module that has 487. About what percentage of the module's files is that? Give a whole number.
hint: Divide 14 by 487 and multiply by 100.

prompt: In `~/mods-vendor`, `go list -m all` failed with `can't compute 'all' using the vendor directory`. Why?
hint: What does `vendor` hold, and what does `all` ask about?

choices.text: The vendor directory was out of date with `go.mod`
choices.why: That failure is `inconsistent vendoring`, and it came later, after `go mod edit`.

choices.text: `GOPROXY=off` was still in effect from the build before
choices.why: A variable set in front of one command lasts for that command only.

choices.text: The `vendor` copy holds packages, not the module graph
choices.why: Right. The graph of section 03 is not in it, and `-mod=mod` reads the module cache instead.

choices.text: `go list` cannot read modules once they are vendored
choices.why: `go list -f "{{.Dir}}"` worked a line earlier and pointed into `vendor`.

prompt: A build machine has no network and an empty module cache. Which module will `go build` compile there with no flags?
hint: What did `GOPROXY=off GOMODCACHE=/nowhere` prove?

choices.text: One with `go.mod` and `go.sum` committed
choices.why: `go.sum` checks bytes it must still fetch; with no network and no cache there is nothing to check.

choices.text: One with an up-to-date `vendor` and a `go` line of 1.14 or later
choices.why: Right. The build reads `vendor` by itself, and `~/mods-vendor` built with downloads forbidden.

choices.text: One whose dependencies are recorded in a `go.work` file
choices.why: A workspace points at local module directories; it does not bring a downloaded dependency along.

choices.text: Any module, as long as `-mod=mod` is set in `GOFLAGS`
choices.why: `-mod=mod` is the setting that ignores `vendor` and asks for the module cache, which is empty here.

prompt: Match each command to what it did in this lesson.
hint: One command per section, and one more from section 03.

pairs.right: Wrote a `go.mod` with a `module` and a `go` line
Copied the needed packages into the module
Checked that the cache had not changed since the download

right_distractors: Upgraded every dependency to its latest release

prompt: Ana commits `~/mods-accents` to a repository. Which belong in the commit? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which files would the next person's build need?

choices.text: `go.mod`
choices.why: Yes: it names the module and the versions it requires.

choices.text: `go.sum`
choices.why: Yes. Without it the next build stops at `missing go.sum entry`, and the hashes have to be taken again.

choices.text: `~/go/pkg/mod/golang.org/x/text@v0.42.0`
choices.why: That is the module cache, outside the module and shared by every module on the machine.

choices.text: The binary `go build` left beside `main.go`
choices.why: A binary is rebuilt from the source; the repository holds what it is built from.

prompt: A vendored module's requirement moved from v0.42.0 to v0.41.0, and `go build` now reports `inconsistent vendoring`. What fixes it?
hint: The new version needs hashes first, then a copy.

choices.text: Deleting `vendor/modules.txt` so the check has nothing to compare
choices.why: Without the index the go command cannot tell what `vendor` holds, and the copy is still of v0.42.0.

choices.text: `go mod tidy` first, then `go mod vendor` again
choices.why: Right: `tidy` adds the new version's lines to `go.sum`, and `vendor` copies it.

choices.text: Editing the version in `modules.txt` by hand
choices.why: The index would then describe v0.41.0 while the files beside it are still v0.42.0.

choices.text: Building with `-mod=vendor` to force the copy to be used
choices.why: The vendor directory was already in use; that is why the mismatch was found.

prompt: The rule that picks the highest of the versions each module asks for, and nothing newer, is minimal version ___.
hint: The English name has three words.
